Jensen closed his GTC Berlin 2026 keynote with this Hermes Agent demo as the finale. 

He introduced it by saying the way to build an agent is to ask an agent to build it for you, so he installed and set up a customized Hermes in one prompt. 

Then he used Hermes, running on @nvidia RTX Spark, to create a simulated training environment for the @huggingface Microduck. Hermes planned an obstacle course with Nemotron and had GPT-6 Astra build it using FreeCAD, Omniverse libraries, Blender, Newton, and Isaac Lab. Hermes trained thousands of simulated ducks on that course until the validated policy was ready to run on the real robot in the physical world.

At Nous, we believe open source is a practical tool as much as a philosophical ideal. It gives users the ability to build powerful, complex workflows chaining numerous local+cloud models, devices, and tools themselves instead of waiting for a company to enable them.

But first, quick recap of what @bulktrade actually is:

Solana validators run a second binary (bulk-agave) next to their normal client, form their own leaderless BFT network (BULKBFT), agree on each batch of orders, and then every validator runs the same deterministic matching engine on the same batch.

Custody stays in a Solana program, so there is no bridge, no sequencer, and no block proposer to bribe. On top sits a portfolio margin engine that prices your full holdings against a live correlation matrix across 9 volatility regimes.

Nobody else on Solana is doing this. Pacifica matches on its own servers offchain, Bullet runs a bonded sequencer, and Phoenix mainly bets on the L1 catching up (which is hard against app-specific designs).

Arcium shipped Blackthorn in private alpha today, and I wrote up why I think it’s the most interesting thing in private AI rn.
TL;DR:
• Venice ($1.3B) still runs its encrypted mode through an Intel TDX enclave, per its own docs. TDX got broken twice in 12 months:
TEE.fail
in Oct 2025, DDRop in Sep 2026. The NVIDIA side survived both.
• Blackthorn is the same GPU stack with the Intel part cut out. Model runs in confidential GPU memory, the session keys sit in MPC, MPC stays off the per-token path. Near-native speed is Arcium’s claim, no benchmark yet.
• It’s infra, not a chat app. API, rented GPUs or self-install. The obvious move is a Venice-style front end on Arcium’s own API.
• Pricing: $ARX $49M mcap / $234M FDV vs $VVV $1.3B / $2.2B. 27x on mcap, 9x on FDV. Infra vs infra it already trades at a 4x FDV premium to Phala, so the market is pricing a shot at the app layer, not cheap TEE infra.
• The gap to $VVV exists bc Blackthorn has no users and no fees yet. If it, or something built on it, attracts real users, that gap closes. That’s my bet.

Venice is a $1.3B bet that people will pay for private AI.

What many don't talk about: its privacy still runs through an Intel chip, and that chip got broken twice in the last 12 months.

@Arcium just shipped the version without that chip, at $49M mcap.

Why does the chip matter?

Venice's encrypted mode runs the model on NVIDIA GPUs with an Intel TDX enclave in front of them (per its own docs), which makes TDX the weak link. TEE(.)fail pulled attestation keys straight off the DDR5 bus in October 2025, and DDRop forged TDX attestation with a $159 interposer in September 2026. The NVIDIA side of things survived both, bc GPU memory sits inside the package where you can't clip a board onto it.

Blackthorn is basically the same stack with the Intel part cut out, shipped as infra: an API, rented GPUs, or self-install on your own Hopper/Blackwell boxes. It's not a consumer-facing chat app in itself.
